canonical_title: We Can Remember It For You Wholesale
author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction, April 1966
card_summary: Douglas Quail, a clerk at the West Coast Emigration Bureau, wants to have gone to Mars and cannot afford to go.
page_summary:
Douglas Quail, a clerk at the West Coast Emigration Bureau, wants to have gone to Mars and cannot afford to go. He buys from Rekal, Incorporated an implanted memory of a trip taken as an Interplan secret agent — the firm's argument being that an implanted recollection is better than a real one, because real memories decay and theirs do not. Under sedation he begins talking, and the technicians discover the implant will not take: he really did go to Mars, really was an Interplan agent, and his authentic memories were erased by the government. The firm refunds half his fee, plants none of the props, and hurries him out. He goes home, finds a box of Martian specimens he cannot account for, and is confronted by Interplan police who have been listening through a transmitter in his skull. What surfaces next is why the memory was erased: he was trained as an assassin and killed a man on Mars. They decide he must be shot immediately; he disarms one and escapes. Unable to hide from a device inside his own head, he offers a bargain — erase the real memories again and implant a fantasy large enough to satisfy him permanently. Interplan psychiatrists find his deepest wish, and it is a childhood one: at nine he met an alien landing party, spared them out of kindness, and they covenanted never to invade Earth while he lives. Back at Rekal, McClane assembles the props for it. Under sedation Quail begins describing the scroll of gratitude the aliens gave him, and where in his conapt it is hidden — along with the invisible destroying rod he used to kill the man on Mars.

**Why it matters.** The story's design is a wish that keeps coming true at the wrong scale. Quail wants to have been an agent; he was one. He then wants a fantasy large enough to hold him; the fantasy he actually harbours is that he personally guarantees the survival of Earth — and that turns out to be true as well. What keeps this from being merely a trick ending twice over is the middle section's argument, made by a salesman and never refuted: that a bought memory is better than a lived one because it does not decay. The story takes seriously the idea that the difference between having done a thing and remembering it may be commercial rather than metaphysical, and then removes the ground from under the distinction by making the corroborating objects real.

*McClane decides to put the props away, reflecting that the genuine article will probably not be long in coming.*

structure.form: short story in three movements, each ending with a discovery that reframes the one before
movements: Rekal: the sales pitch, the sedation, and the discovery that the fantasy is a fact.
The pursuit: the transmitter, the assassination surfacing, the escape, the bargain.
The second implantation: the childhood fantasy identified, the props assembled, and the second reversal.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Quail and McClane. Putting the reader in the vendor's office as often as in the customer's head is what makes the machinery of memory feel like a business rather than a metaphysics.
structure.structural_joke: The story runs the same scene twice — the intercom buzzing, McClane sprinting to the work area, the technician saying 'he reacted well to the narkidrine' — and the repetition is the point. The second discovery lands in exactly the shape of the first.

characters.name: Douglas Quail
characters.note: His wish is stated in the first line and granted three times over in forms he cannot survive. Notably, he is never shown to be lying or deluded; every implausible thing he says turns out to be true.

characters.name: McClane
characters.note: Sells memory as a superior product to experience, on the reasonable ground that real recollection decays. He is competent, decent enough to refund, and perspires steadily from the moment the trade goes wrong.

characters.name: Kirsten Quail
characters.note: Derisive throughout and gone by the middle of the story. Quail briefly wonders whether she is an Interplan minder; the story never answers.

characters.name: Lowe and Keeler
characters.note: Deliver both reversals. Keeler's objection — that grafting a false memory over a real one would force the man to hold two opposite premises at once — is the story's own description of its subject.

characters.name: The Interplan police
characters.note: Communicate by transmitter inside Quail's skull and answer his thoughts before he speaks them. Their sympathy at the end is real and does not alter the standing order to kill him.

settings.name: Rekal, Incorporated, Chicago
settings.note: A small pink building with a shifting neon sign, a vault of packets, and standard operating procedure for planting corroborating props in a client's apartment.

settings.name: Mars
settings.note: Never shown. It exists as a want in the first line, as a set of memories that may be manufactured, and as a box of dried specimens in a desk drawer.

settings.name: Quail's conapt
settings.note: Where the proofs of each successive story are found, and where the next set will be planted.

motifs: Proof as merchandise: ticket stubs, postcards, a spoon engraved with a Martian address — corroboration sold by the packet
The transmitter in the skull, which makes thought itself a form of speech that can be held against him
Refund as the measure of the firm's alarm — half returned, then the balance, then none of the props
Two premises held at once, named by a technician as a psychiatric danger and then delivered as the plot

distinctive_terms.label: Covenant
distinctive_terms.note: The aliens' covenant not to invade while Quail lives — the story's theological register, arriving in its last pages.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's recorded remarks are entirely commercial — the film option, listed among four deals — with no statement of what he thought the story was doing.

evidence.quote: there are my MOVIE DEALS, all four of them: on Second Variety, We Can Remember It For You Wholesale, Do…
evidence.reading: Listing options in progress. The same letter run covers the Claw option on Second Variety, so the two dossiers share a moment in his career.

evidence.quote: My story "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" is being made into a film
evidence.reading: Reported alongside Bantam's print run figures — the letter is about money and reach, not about meaning.

pkd_on_this_work.gap_noted: No interpretive statement by Dick about this story appears in the archive, which is unusual for a work of this standing. Worth searching the interviews in The Shifting Realities of Philip K. Dick.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: the dazzling reality inversions of a story such as "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale"
evidence.reading: Palmer treats the story as the exemplary case of a technique rather than as a thesis.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: further revelations and mysteries in turn displace the object of quest from the centre of the narrative
evidence.reading: A precise description of what the second ending does: the Mars assassination, having been the revelation, is displaced by the childhood covenant.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: the Disney Studios would exercise its option on Total Recall, a screenplay based on Phil's 1966 story
evidence.reading: Establishes the adaptation history and that the option was live in Dick's lifetime.

open_questions: The archive holds no statement by Dick about what this story means, only about its film prospects. The Shifting Realities interviews are the likeliest place for one and have not been searched at the passage level.
Quail wonders whether his wife is an Interplan minder and the story drops it. Is there a draft or a letter indicating whether that thread was cut?
Sutin notes The Preserving Machine is the only collection to carry this story. Worth confirming against the bibliographies, since it bears on which readers encountered it before the film.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
